title: The Count of Monte Cristo
author: Alexandre Dumas
description: It opens in the old harbour of Marseille, where the Pharaon docks and Edmond Dantès is arrested, and at the Château d'If, the real island fortress off the coast where he is buried alive for fourteen years. His escape and the treasure carry the story out of France: to the island of Monte Cristo in the Tuscan archipelago, and to Rome, before he returns to take his revenge in Paris. The Italian and Roman scenes are flagged as excursions beyond the setting.

route.summary: The novel opens here on 24 February 1815, as nineteen-year-old Edmond Dantès brings the Pharaon home to Marseille. Within hours he is betrayed and arrested at his own betrothal feast. The old harbour is where his life is taken from him, and where, an ageless fortune later, the Count returns to close his accounts.
route.note: The Pharaon is steered into the inner port of Marseille, the Vieux-Port at the foot of the Canebière, which is real and named through the chapter. The pin marks the old harbour.

route.summary: Mercédès, the Catalan girl Dantès is to marry, lives in this fishing colony on the edge of Marseille. It is here that his rival Fernand nurses the jealousy that helps send Edmond to prison, and here that Mercédès waits, and finally gives up waiting.
route.note: Dumas places the Catalan settlement on a promontory just outside Marseille; the real village des Catalans stood in the Saint-Lambert cove, now the Plage des Catalans in the 7th arrondissement. The pin marks that cove.

route.summary: Dantès is rowed out to the island fortress and locked in a dungeon for fourteen years. Here he meets the Abbé Faria, who educates him and reveals the hidden treasure, and from here he escapes, sewn into a shroud and flung into the sea, to become the Count of Monte Cristo.
route.note: The Château d'If is a real fortress on the Île d'If in the Frioul archipelago off Marseille, named repeatedly in the text. It lies within the book's setting, off the coast.

route.summary: On the barren Tuscan island that will give him his title, Dantès digs out Cardinal Spada's treasure in a hidden cave. The fortune of gold coin, gold bars and jewels makes the escaped prisoner immeasurably rich and turns Edmond Dantès into the Count of Monte Cristo, the instrument of his own long revenge.
route.note: Montecristo is a real island in the Tuscan archipelago, off the Italian coast south of Elba, named in the title and the text. It lies in Italy, well outside the French setting, so it is flagged as an excursion.

route.summary: In Rome for the carnival, Franz and Albert visit the Colosseum by moonlight, where Franz overhears the mysterious Count arranging a bandit's pardon. Days later, when the carnival on the Corso ends with Albert kidnapped by Luigi Vampa, the Count is the one man who can, and does, save him, binding the young Parisian to him for the revenge to come.
route.note: The Colosseum in Rome is real and named in the text. Rome lies in Italy, outside the French setting, so it is flagged as an excursion.

route.summary: The Count arrives in Paris and takes a mansion on the Champs-Élysées, the stage for the last third of the book. From here, moving among the men who ruined him, now grown rich and respectable, he draws Danglars, Fernand and Villefort one by one into the ruin he has spent his fortune preparing.
route.note: The Champs-Élysées is a real Paris avenue, named in the text; the Count's specific house on it is invented. The pin marks a point on the avenue near the Rue de Ponthieu, where Dumas sets the house.
